title: Monitoring air quality index with EWMA and individual charts using XGBoost and SVR residuals
author: Alfasanah, Niam, et al.
materials: The Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) chart's design is characterized by two primary parameters: the sigma multiplier for control limits (L) and the weighting factor (λ). Optimal selection of L and λ is crucial for attaining the desired Average Run Length (ARL). The selection of these two parameters is important because EWMA is capable of detecting small shifts. Therefore, this method is suitable for cases with frequent changes, such as air quality monitoring. Empirical evidence suggests that a weighting factor within the interval 0.05 ≤ λ ≤ 0.25 generally yields satisfactory performance. The EWMA is a prevalent technique in time series analysis and prediction [29]. The EWMA's computation, which incorporates a weighted average of historical and current data points, renders it relatively insensitive to departures from normality. Consequently, it is a robust control charting technique for monitoring individual observations.

The air quality index data for each phase is modeled using Support Vector Regression (SVR) to address autocorrelation. After organizing the data into input variable compositions, the optimal hyperparameter values for the SVR model are determined according to the kernel type used. The kernels employed in this study are Radial Basis Function (RBF) and Polynomial kernels. For the Radial Basis Function kernel, the hyperparameters considered are C and σ. Specifically, the values of the hyperparameter C (cost) used are 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100, while the values of the hyperparameter σ (sigma) used are 0.01, 1, and 5. Based on these specified hyperparameter values, there are 15 combinations of hyperparameters for the Radial Basis Function kernel that will be used in a grid search to produce the best model with the smallest RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) value. In the testing stage, the application of the EWMA control chart with varying lambda values showed a shift in the process that was not detected in the training stage. In particular, with λ = 0.4, one residual point that was outside the control limits (out-of-control, OOC) was detected (See Fig. 14). This detection indicates a moderate shift in the test data. This needs to be investigated further, and the cause should be determined whether it is due to the dry season or the increase in temperature. Furthermore, it is important to note that Southeast Asia, including Jakarta, experienced a significant heatwave from March to April. This heatwave could have contributed to the observed shift in the data. The extreme temperatures during this period may have affected air quality and increased the levels of particulate matter (PM 2.5), leading to the out-of-control point detected in the EWMA control chart. This potential impact of the heatwave underscores the need for a thorough investigation into the underlying causes of the process shift. steps.title: Collect and split AQI data
steps.instruction: Download PM2.5‑based Air Quality Index data from the AQICN platform for the period 1 Jan 2023 – 31 May 2024. Partition the dataset into Phase I (training) covering 1 Jan 2023 – 31 Dec 2023) and Phase II (testing) covering 1 Jan 2024 – 31 May 2024.

steps.title: Assess autocorrelation
steps.instruction: Plot the Autocorrelation Function (ACF) of the PM2.5 series to confirm the presence of autocorrelation (noted for lags 1‑37).

steps.title: Identify significant lags
steps.instruction: Plot the Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF) with a 0.05 significance level and select the lags that exceed the confidence bounds: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8. Use these lags as input variables (y₍i‑1₎, y₍i‑2₎, y₍i‑4₎, y₍i‑5₎, y₍i‑8₎) for all subsequent models.

steps.title: Prepare modeling environment
steps.instruction: Install R 4.1.2 and load the packages caret, xgboost, e1071, kernlab, qcc, and ggplot2 for data preprocessing, model training, validation, and charting.

steps.title: Train XGBoost model
steps.instruction: Using the Phase I data and the selected lagged inputs, train an XGBoost regression model with maximum tree depth 3 and 50 boosting rounds (nrounds = 50).

steps.title: Tune SVR hyper‑parameters
steps.instruction: Perform a grid‑search with time‑series cross‑validation (no shuffling) on Phase I data for two kernel types.

substeps.instruction: RBF kernel: test C = 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100 and σ = 0.01, 1, 5 (15 combinations). Select the combination with the smallest RMSE (C = 10, σ = 0.01; RMSE = 17.155).
Polynomial kernel: test C = 0.01, 0.1, 1, 100; degree d = 1‑5; coefficient r = 0.001, 0.01, 0.1 (60 combinations). Select the best (C = 100, d = 1, r = 0.001; RMSE = 17.167).

steps.title: Evaluate model performance
steps.instruction:
Compute Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) with 95 % confidence intervals for both models on Phase I (training) and Phase II (testing):
- XGBoost: Phase I RMSE = 9.87 [9.10, 10.57]; Phase II RMSE = 20.38 [17.99, 22.47]
- SVR (RBF): Phase I RMSE = 17.16 [15.69, 18.69]; Phase II RMSE = 18.85 [16.95, 20.78]

steps.title: Generate residual series
steps.instruction: For each model (XGBoost and SVR) and each phase, calculate residuals = observed AQI – predicted AQI. Store four residual series: XGBoost‑Phase I, XGBoost‑Phase II, SVR‑Phase I, SVR‑Phase II.

steps.title: Create Individual control charts
steps.instruction: Using the qcc package, plot Individual (Shewhart) control charts for each residual series. Compute the average (x̄), average moving range (MR̄), and control limits UCL = x̄ + 3·MR̄/d₂, LCL = x̄ − 3·MR̄/d₂ (d₂ for n = 2). Record out‑of‑control (OOC) points:

steps.title: Create EWMA control charts
steps.instruction: For each residual series, plot EWMA charts with weighting factors λ = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4. Use Z₀ = μ₀ (overall mean) and control limits UCL = μ₀ + L·σ·√[λ/(2‑λ)] and LCL = μ₀ − L·σ·√[λ/(2‑λ)], where L is the sigma multiplier. Record OOC points:

substeps.instruction: XGBoost Phase I: 0 OOC points for all λ
XGBoost Phase II: 1 OOC point at λ = 0.4
SVR Phase I: 0 OOC points for all λ
SVR Phase II: 0 OOC points for all λ

steps.title: Compare chart sensitivities
steps.instruction:
Summarize the OOC counts from Table 8:
- XGBoost + Individual: 0 (Phase I), 22 (Phase II)
- XGBoost + EWMA: 0 (Phase I), 1 (Phase II)
- SVR + Individual: 6 (Phase I), 0 (Phase II)
- SVR + EWMA: 0 (Phase I), 0 (Phase II)
Conclude that XGBoost combined with EWMA provides the best balance of stability (no false alarms in Phase I) and sensitivity (detects a single moderate shift in Phase II).

steps.title: Interpret monitoring results
steps.instruction: For any OOC point, investigate potential causes (e.g., heatwave March‑April 2024, industrial activity, traffic, weather). Use the identified shift to trigger further data collection or corrective actions in air‑quality management.
